newsitem.title: GERMANY: Three men head list of possible Kohl successors. [CORRECTED 16:18 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Three men head list of possible Kohl successors. [CORRECTED 16:18 GMT]

text.p: As speculation continues about whether German Chancellor Helmut Kohl will decide to step down this year, three men head the pack of possible successors: his closest aide Wolfgang Schaeuble, Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber and Defence Minister Volker Ruehe.

None is likely to make a serious move until Kohl, in power for 14 years, decides whether or not to stand in the October 1998 general election -- something he has promised to ponder after an EU summit in June.
But all have discreetly moved themselves into position for a crack at the top job, if not sooner then later.

Unquestioned favourite and Kohl's preferred candidate is Wolfgang Schaeuble, 54, the chancellor's trusty lieutenant and trouble-shooter for his entire tenure, who has been confined to a wheelchair since being shot by a deranged man (corrects from "woman") in 1990.

The attack came just a week after the German unification ceremony which crowned Schaeuble's greatest achievement, the negotiation of the treaty which brought together capitalist West Germany and the formerly communist East.

Within weeks, Schaeuble was back at his desk as Interior Minister, then switching to his current post as head of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) in parliament, maintaining iron discipline and often drawing fire aimed at the chancellor.

Schaeuble's unquestioned loyalty to Kohl -- and the affection which saw Kohl weep at his bedside after the attack -- has earned him the chancellor's blessing to move into position as a possible successor.
A poll in the weekly Der Spiegel said 40 percent of Germans saw Schaeuble as the best conservative successor to Kohl, with 24 percent for Stoiber and 14 percent for Ruehe.
Despite his often abrasive manner with colleagues and opponents alike, and his disability, Schaeuble outscored his rivals on every characteristic except physical fitness.

Even that has become less of an issue for ordinary Germans as Schaeuble has steadily stripped away the taboos surrounding paralysis, even going so far as to say in his autobiography that it was possible for a paraplegic to have a sex life of sorts.

In an interview last month with the magazine Stern, he staked his clearest claim yet to be chancellor one day, saying it was a temptation he could probably not refuse and adding that it was fair for Germans to ask if a "cripple" could do the job.

If Schaeuble does not get the job, he is sure to have a big say in who does -- something that could be an obstacle to the ambition of Bavaria's workaholic and openly ambitious premier Edmund Stoiber, 55.

Stoiber's chancellery credentials stem from his success in dragging Bavaria's Christian Social Union (CSU) out of a mire of corruption scandals with puritanical zeal, and shored up an absolute conservative majority in Germany's biggest state.
But he attracts suspicion from many Bonn politicians for his readiness to don traditional costume and espouse populist causes at the drop of a feathered hat.

Owing no allegiance to Kohl and giving little loyalty to his own CSU chairman and Bonn finance minister, Theo Waigel, Stoiber has also played to ordinary German fears of an EU single currency by making himself the most prominent conservative critic of EU monetary union.
What may cost him dearest, however, is a careless remark in Schaeuble's direction that no invalid could ever be chancellor.
Less of an outsider is Volker Ruehe, 54.

The bullish English teacher has earned his spurs by skilfully persuading Germans -- and not least the leftist opposition -- to give up long-cherished scruples and agree to let German troops go on missions abroad.
Like Schaeuble, Ruehe has done much dirty work for the chancellor, mostly during a spell as party general secretary before 1992.
Since alienating many in the coalition with frequent interference in foreign affairs, he has channelled his obvious ambitions into his own area with no less effect.

Unfortunately for his prospects, his power base in the CDU in the city of Hamburg is too small to carry him to the chancellery, and he would almost certainly need Schaeuble's support for a bid for the top job
